marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q001.takeaway: Chloride ions activate salivary α-amylase and support starch hydrolysis.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q001.displayText:
Chloride ions activate salivary α-amylase and support starch hydrolysis.

Salivary amylase is activated by Cl-.

Human salivary and pancreatic amylases are activated by chloride (Cl-). They have optimum activities near-neutral pH (7.4). They hydrolyze internal 1:4° linkages but spare 1:6° linkages and terminal 1:4° linkages in starch.
emphasis: Chloride ions activate salivary α-amylase and support starch hydrolysis

rationales.a: Sodium is not the principal activating ion for ptyalin.
rationales.b: Potassium is not the key amylase activator.
rationales.c: Bicarbonate buffers saliva but chloride is the recognized enzyme activator.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q002.takeaway: Brush-border enzymes in the small intestine hydrolyze disaccharides to absorbable monosaccharides.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q002.displayText:
Brush-border enzymes in the small intestine hydrolyze disaccharides to absorbable monosaccharides.

Digestion of disaccharides occurs in the small intestine.

The enzymes maltase, sucrase, isomaltase, lactase, and trehalase are located in the enterocytes covering the intestinal microvilli brush border. The disaccharides are digested into their constituent monosaccharides as they come in contact with these enterocytes.
emphasis: Brush-border enzymes in the small intestine hydrolyze disaccharides to absorbable monosaccharides

rationales.a: The mouth begins polysaccharide digestion, but brush-border disaccharidases act in small intestine.
rationales.b: The acidic stomach is not the primary site of disaccharide hydrolysis.
rationales.d: Large intestine primarily absorbs water/electrolytes and ferments residual fiber.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q003.takeaway: Intestinal glucose uptake uses SGLT1 secondary active transport driven by the Na⁺ gradient.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q003.displayText:
Intestinal glucose uptake uses SGLT1 secondary active transport driven by the Na⁺ gradient.

Glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport.

On the basolateral side, there is active transport of sodium ions out of the cell into the interstitial fluid. This depletes sodium inside the cell. Because of this Na+ concentration difference, more Na+ binds to the SGLT on the luminal side. This increases the affinity of SGLT for glucose and glucose binds to it.

Then, both the Na+ and glucose are transported together to the interior of the cell. Thus, glucose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport. The energy for glucose transport is provided indirectly, by the active transport of Na+ out of the cell. The glucose moves out of the cell into the blood across the basolateral membrane by facilitated diffusion mediated via GLUT.
emphasis: Intestinal glucose uptake uses SGLT1 secondary active transport driven by the Na⁺ gradient

rationales.a: Glucose transport is not directly ATP-driven at the apical cotransporter.
rationales.c: Facilitated diffusion applies to basolateral exit via GLUT2, not apical absorption.
rationales.d: The apical mechanism is specifically Na⁺-coupled secondary active uptake, not any pathway.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q004.takeaway: Enterocyte GLUT2 transports absorbed glucose across the basolateral membrane into interstitial fluid.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q004.displayText:
Enterocyte GLUT2 transports absorbed glucose across the basolateral membrane into interstitial fluid.

GLUT2 is involved in the transport of glucose from the enterocyte into the interstitium (or out of the enterocytes).

The image below shows the function of GLUT 2 on enterocytes.

Option A: Fructose absorption is through facilitated diffusion from the intestinal lumen into the enterocyte by GLUT5 and out of the enterocytes into the interstitium by GLUT2.

Option B: SGLT1 is involved in the absorption of glucose into the enterocyte. SGLT2 is responsible for glucose transport out of the renal tubules.

Option D: GLUT1 is responsible for basal glucose uptake in many organs.
emphasis: Enterocyte GLUT2 transports absorbed glucose across the basolateral membrane into interstitial fluid

rationales.a: Fructose enters by GLUT5 facilitated diffusion, not secondary active transport.
rationales.b: SGLT1, not renal SGLT2, mediates intestinal glucose/galactose uptake.
rationales.d: GLUT4 is insulin-regulated in muscle/adipose; basal uptake in many organs uses GLUT1.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q005.takeaway: Isomaltase hydrolyzes α-1,6 branch linkages in starch-derived dextrins.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q005.displayText:
Isomaltase hydrolyzes α-1,6 branch linkages in starch-derived dextrins.

The main enzyme involved in the hydrolysis of 1,6° linkage of starch is isomaltase.

Both salivary and the pancreatic α-amylases hydrolyze internal 1:4° linkages but spare 1:6° linkages and terminal 1:4° linkages of starch.
emphasis: Isomaltase hydrolyzes α-1,6 branch linkages in starch-derived dextrins

rationales.a: Maltase primarily hydrolyzes α-1,4 maltose linkages.
rationales.c: Sucrase hydrolyzes sucrose and some α-1,4 bonds, not the branch α-1,6 linkage.
rationales.d: Lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q006.takeaway: Chymotrypsinogen is the inactive pancreatic zymogen precursor activated to chymotrypsin in the intestinal lumen.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q006.displayText:
Chymotrypsinogen is the inactive pancreatic zymogen precursor activated to chymotrypsin in the intestinal lumen.

Chymotrypsinogen is a zymogen.

Zymogens (proenzymes) are inactive precursors of the enzymes. Most of the peptidases (proteases) are present in the form of proenzymes. Trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase A, procarboxypeptidase B are zymogens.
emphasis: Chymotrypsinogen is the inactive pancreatic zymogen precursor activated to chymotrypsin in the intestinal lumen

rationales.b: Carboxypeptidase is an active exopeptidase enzyme, not chymotrypsinogen.
rationales.c: Transaminase is an intracellular amino-acid metabolism enzyme.
rationales.d: Elastase is a distinct pancreatic protease, secreted as proelastase.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q007.takeaway: Enteropeptidase initiates trypsinogen activation by cleaving a short activation peptide; trypsin then activates other zymogens.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q007.displayText:
Enteropeptidase initiates trypsinogen activation by cleaving a short activation peptide; trypsin then activates other zymogens.

Trypsinogen is converted to trypsin by the removal of a few amino acids.

All proenzymes are converted to their active form by selective proteolysis (removal of a few amino acids).

Enterokinase cleaves trypsinogen to yield active trypsin. It is located on the brush border of duodenal enterocytes.
emphasis: Enteropeptidase initiates trypsinogen activation by cleaving a short activation peptide; trypsin then activates other zymogens

rationales.a: Two trypsin molecules do not combine to form trypsin; activation is proteolytic cleavage.
rationales.b: Phosphorylation is not the activation mechanism for trypsinogen.
rationales.d: Adding an alkali group is not a protease-activation process.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q008.takeaway: Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive proenzymes, preventing autodigestion before intestinal activation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q008.displayText:
Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive proenzymes, preventing autodigestion before intestinal activation.

The synthesis and secretion of proteases as catalytically inactive proenzymes protect the normal pancreas from autodigestion.

All the protease proenzymes present in the pancreatic juice get converted to their active form only in the small intestinal lumen (site of action).

If proenzymes get activated in the pancreas (site of origin), they can digest the entire pancreas within a few hours, giving rise to the condition called acute pancreatitis.
emphasis: Pancreatic proteases are secreted as inactive proenzymes, preventing autodigestion before intestinal activation

rationales.a: Bicarbonate protects the duodenum from acid but does not prevent pancreatic protease autodigestion.
rationales.b: Pancreatic trypsin inhibitor adds protection, but the primary broad safeguard is zymogen secretion.
rationales.d: Pancreatic cells are not inherently resistant to their active proteases; compartmentalization and zymogens protect them.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q009.takeaway: Carboxypeptidase cleaves terminal amino acids and is an exopeptidase; trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase are endopeptidases.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q009.displayText:
Carboxypeptidase cleaves terminal amino acids and is an exopeptidase; trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase are endopeptidases.

Carboxypeptidase is an exopeptidase, not endopeptidase.

Peptidases (proteases) are of two types:
• Endopeptidases - they act at interior peptide bonds in the peptide molecules. Ex- pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase.
• Exopeptidases - they hydrolyze the amino acids at the carboxyl ends of the polypeptides, one at a time. Ex- carboxypeptidase, aminopeptidase.
emphasis: Carboxypeptidase cleaves terminal amino acids and is an exopeptidase; trypsin, chymotrypsin and elastase are endopeptidases

rationales.a: Trypsin cleaves internal peptide bonds, so it is an endopeptidase.
rationales.c: Elastase cleaves internal bonds near small neutral residues.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q010.takeaway: PEPT1 cotransports dipeptides and tripeptides into enterocytes with H⁺; free amino acids use separate carriers.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q010.displayText:
PEPT1 cotransports dipeptides and tripeptides into enterocytes with H⁺; free amino acids use separate carriers.

Peptide transporter 1 (PepT1) is involved in the absorption of the dipeptide.

The dipeptides and tripeptides are transported along with H+ into enterocytes by a system known as peptide transporter 1 (PepT1).

These peptides undergo intracellular hydrolysis to release amino acids. These amino acids are absorbed into the circulation from the basolateral membrane via basolateral amino acid transporter. H+ moves out of the cell via Na+-H+ exchanger on the luminal side.
emphasis: PEPT1 cotransports dipeptides and tripeptides into enterocytes with H⁺; free amino acids use separate carriers

rationales.a: PEPT1 transports small peptides rather than intact polypeptides.
rationales.c: Amino acids are absorbed by amino-acid carriers, not PEPT1.
rationales.d: Immunoglobulin A is not absorbed by PEPT1.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q011.takeaway: Dietary lipids enter enterocytes largely by passive diffusion from micelles, unlike carrier-coupled glucose and amino acids.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q011.displayText:
Dietary lipids enter enterocytes largely by passive diffusion from micelles, unlike carrier-coupled glucose and amino acids.

Lipids are passively absorbed in the gut.

The products of lipid digestion (monoglycerides and free fatty acids) are incorporated into micelles that are formed by bile salts and diffuse across the intestinal epithelium. Short and medium-chain fatty acids can directly diffuse across the intestinal epithelium.

Note: Recent evidence suggests that specific carrier proteins (membrane transporters) may be involved in the transport of long-chain fatty acids.
emphasis: Dietary lipids enter enterocytes largely by passive diffusion from micelles, unlike carrier-coupled glucose and amino acids

rationales.a: Glucose uptake uses SGLT1 secondary active transport.
rationales.b: Galactose also uses sodium-coupled active uptake.
rationales.d: Amino acids use specific carrier-mediated transport.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q012.takeaway: Colonic epithelium absorbs bacterially produced short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q012.displayText:
Colonic epithelium absorbs bacterially produced short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate.

Short-chain fatty acids produced by bacteria are absorbed maximally in the colon by secondary active transport.

Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum.

Folate is absorbed in the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).

Maximum water absorption takes place in the jejunum.
emphasis: Colonic epithelium absorbs bacterially produced short-chain fatty acids, especially butyrate

rationales.a: Duodenum is not the main site for SCFA absorption from bacterial fermentation.
rationales.b: Jejunum absorbs nutrients but receives less colonic fermentation product.
rationales.c: Ileum can absorb some SCFAs, but the colon is their principal site of production and uptake.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q013.takeaway: Colonic short-chain fatty acids fuel colonocytes, support barrier integrity and help acid-base/electrolyte balance; they do not cause Na⁺ secretion.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q013.displayText:
Colonic short-chain fatty acids fuel colonocytes, support barrier integrity and help acid-base/electrolyte balance; they do not cause Na⁺ secretion.

Short-chain fatty acids (2-5-carbon) in the colon promote the absorption of Na+, not secretion.

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) in the colon are formed by the action of colonic bacteria on complex carbohydrates, resistant starches, and other components of the dietary fiber i.e the material that escapes digestion in the upper gastrointestinal tract and enters the colon.

Functions:
• Exert a trophic effect on the colonic epithelial cells
• Combat inflammation
• Helps in maintaining acid-base equilibrium
emphasis: Colonic short-chain fatty acids fuel colonocytes, support barrier integrity and help acid-base/electrolyte balance; they do not cause Na⁺ secretion

rationales.a: Butyrate has a trophic and energy-supplying effect on colonic epithelial cells.
rationales.b: SCFAs can reinforce barrier function and reduce inflammation.
rationales.c: SCFA absorption and metabolism influence colonic pH and acid-base balance.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q014.takeaway: Jejunal resection most threatens major fluid/electrolyte absorption because it removes a large area of small-intestinal absorptive surface.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q014.displayText:
Jejunal resection most threatens major fluid/electrolyte absorption because it removes a large area of small-intestinal absorptive surface.

The resection of jejunum leads to major electrolyte imbalance because most of the fluid and electrolyte reabsorption occurs in this segment.

The maximum water absorption takes place in the jejunum.

The amount of water absorbed in the intestines follows this order: Jejunum > Ileum > Colon.

Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum.

Folate is absorbed in the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).
emphasis: Jejunal resection most threatens major fluid/electrolyte absorption because it removes a large area of small-intestinal absorptive surface

rationales.a: Duodenal resection can impair iron/calcium uptake but is shorter and may be partly compensated.
rationales.c: Ileal resection causes B12/bile-salt malabsorption, but the item’s major bulk fluid-loss risk is jejunal loss.
rationales.d: Sigmoid resection removes a limited colonic segment and usually spares most fluid absorption.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q015.takeaway: About 8 L of fluid is absorbed daily by the intestine from ingested fluid and gastrointestinal secretions.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q015.displayText:
About 8 L of fluid is absorbed daily by the intestine from ingested fluid and gastrointestinal secretions.

The amount of fluid absorbed in the intestine in a day is around 8L.

About 2L of ingested water and 7L of various secretions enter the gastrointestinal tract. Out of this, the majority (8800 mL) is absorbed in the small intestine and colon. The small remaining volume that is not absorbed (100-200 mL) is excreted in feces.
emphasis: About 8 L of fluid is absorbed daily by the intestine from ingested fluid and gastrointestinal secretions

rationales.a: 5 L underestimates the approximate total load reabsorbed.
rationales.b: 11 L exceeds the usual daily intestinal fluid absorption estimate.
rationales.c: 2 L accounts mainly for intake and ignores secreted digestive fluids.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q016.takeaway: The colon absorbs sodium, chloride and short-chain fatty acids but secretes potassium into the lumen.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q016.displayText:
The colon absorbs sodium, chloride and short-chain fatty acids but secretes potassium into the lumen.

K+ is not absorbed in the colon. It is secreted in the rectal fluid.

Electrolytes (Na+, Cl-), short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate), and water are absorbed in the colon.
emphasis: The colon absorbs sodium, chloride and short-chain fatty acids but secretes potassium into the lumen

rationales.a: Acetate is a short-chain fatty acid absorbed by the colon.
rationales.b: Chloride is absorbed along with sodium in colonic epithelium.
rationales.c: Sodium is actively absorbed, including via ENaC in distal colon.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q017.takeaway: Folate uptake uses proton-coupled transporters; the claim that folate carriers are Na⁺ cotransporters is false.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q017.displayText:
Folate uptake uses proton-coupled transporters; the claim that folate carriers are Na⁺ cotransporters is false.

Folate and vitamin B12 absorption is Na+-independent.

The remaining water-soluble vitamins—thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, pyridoxine, pantothenate, biotin, and ascorbic acid are absorbed by carriers that are Na+ cotransporters.

Option A: Fat-soluble vitamins are ingested in the form of esters. Digestion needs hydrolysis by cholesterol esterase and absorbed after incorporating into micelles.

Options B and D: Most vitamins are absorbed in the upper small intestine, but vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum. Vitamin B12 binds to intrinsic factor, a protein secreted by the parietal cells of the stomach. This complex is absorbed across the ileal mucosa.
emphasis: Folate uptake uses proton-coupled transporters; the claim that folate carriers are Na⁺ cotransporters is false

rationales.a: Fat-soluble vitamin absorption can depend on lipid digestion and micelle formation.
rationales.b: Vitamin B₁₂–intrinsic-factor complex is absorbed in terminal ileum.
rationales.d: Many water-soluble vitamins are absorbed in proximal small intestine.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q018.takeaway: Non-heme iron is absorbed primarily in the duodenum, where reduction and DMT1-mediated uptake occur.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH32_Q018.displayText:
Non-heme iron is absorbed primarily in the duodenum, where reduction and DMT1-mediated uptake occur.

Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

Most of the iron in the diet is in the ferric (Fe3+) form, whereas it is the ferrous (Fe2+) form that is absorbed.

Note: Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids are absorbed throughout the length of the small intestine. Bile acids are present throughout the small intestine, but active absorption occurs only in the ileum, and active absorption of folate occurs in the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).
emphasis: Non-heme iron is absorbed primarily in the duodenum, where reduction and DMT1-mediated uptake occur

rationales.b: Jejunum can absorb some iron, but duodenum is the principal site.
rationales.c: Ileum is the site for B12/bile-salt uptake, not most iron.
rationales.d: Stomach acid helps solubilize iron but absorption occurs mainly in duodenum.
